comment_text: Can politicians opposing Covaxin explain the death of a nurse with no prior preconditions in Portugal after receiving the Pfizer vaccine? Let this idiocy stop. On advise of Indian scientists and scientists of Indian origin from abroad, the government has allowed Covaxin to collect more data of efficacy in vaccination program in a trial mode. To further clarify, only the vaccines from Astra Zeneca (Covishield), Pfizer and Moderna have efficacy data, but that was conducted on a small cohort size of a few thousand people and means nothing. While Pfizer and Moderna use the novel mRNA technology, Astra Zeneca uses Chimpanzee Adenovirus for gene delivery. On the other hand, Covaxin uses a much more proven technique (akin to pulse polio) and immune system gets the opportunity to recognize a much bigger array of SARS-CoV2 epitopes. This theoretically should give a wider range of protection, especially given the fact that multiple new strains are emerging. All the 4 vaccines have shown various levels (and encouraging levels) of immune response and people must get vaccinated. Humanity has suffered a lot. These are all first generation vaccines, and their real efficacies, counter indications and how long can they give protection can only be judged only after tens of thousand people are vaccinated and response is monitored over a period of 1 year. This is a learning process for scientists and doctors. Given the aggressiveness of the disease, if we go on the path of how MERS vaccine is being tested, we would have lost millions of lives. Since safety has been established in trials, it is important that people get vaccinated to stop the pandemic or at least slow it down. Yes, despite trials on safety, there can be counter-indications as happened with Pfizer vaccine in one case so far. Scientists will investigate and learn from it. But for some exceptional cases, the whole humanity can not be put under risk. Even scientists are afraid that the vaccines of Pfizer, Moderna and Astra Zeneca may not be as effective against mutant strains. Covaxin might actually give the cover there as it uses a very wide array of epitopes. I hope this helps. This wide world has many renowned scientists to guide people on this serious issue.

किसानों, कारीगरों और फोजी. हमें एक सहयोगी स्थानीय अर्थव्यवस्था और संस्कृति का निर्माण करना होगा। हमारे भोजन, कपड़े, दवाइयों, निर्माण सामग्री, बिजली स्थानीय स्तर पर उत्पादन करना होगा। या छोटे पड़ोसी उत्पादक से सीधे खरीदना होगा।स्थानीय प्रशासन खुद् चलाएं, किसी भी राजनेता को भाग लेने की अनुमति नहीं दी। बड़ी कंपनी से कुछ भी नहीं खरीदना चाहिए। टीके शरीर की प्राकृतिक प्रतिरक्षा की नकल करने का एक असफल प्रयास है। और अक्सर यह हमारे शरीर की प्राकृतिक प्रतिरक्षा और उपचार तंत्र को नुकसान पहुंचाता है। हमें क्षेत्रीय- मौसमी फल और सब्जियां और मुख्य रूप से पौधों पर आधारित पूरे वाले खाद्य पदार्थ (plant based whole foods) और किसी भी प्रसंस्कृत, पैकेज्ड कारखाने से बने खाद्य पदार्थों या उपकरण बहिष्कार ( avoid any processed, packaged factory made food or ingredient) करके अपनी प्रतिरक्षा प्रणाली को बढ़ावा देने की आवश्यकता है। धूप में निकलें, सामाजिक जीवन, सांस्कृतिक गतिविधियों, नृत्य और आउटडोर खेलों या तैराकी का आनंद लें। सरल  😄

title: Covid-19: Update on Vaccines and Implications of the New Variants
comment_text: The order of importance in dealing with COIVD is stopping deaths, hospitalizations and then infections. So far, every vaccine with phase 3 trial results has stopped both hospitalizations and deaths, regardless of how effective they are in stopping symptomatic infections. No vaccinated person in a phase 3 trial for the Pfizer, Moderna, or Astro-Zeneca vaccine has ended up in hospital or has died from COVID.   In the province of Ontario, Canada with about 15 million people 70% of covid deaths over the last year are for those over 80, and 25% for those between 60 and 80. The percentage of the population over 80 is about 5%, and between 60 and 80 about 20%. These death statistics and population distribution are likely very similar in most developed countries. Therefore, when every older person is vaccinated then once the vaccines take effect hospitalizations and deaths from COVID should decline by around 90 to 95%. That should stop the overloading of the medical system, and in fact it is critical that this actually happens.   Since millions are now being vaccinated it is easy to verify that for the vast majority the vaccines stop hospitalization and deaths simply by checking if a new COVID patient has already been vaccinated. In Israel about 60% of people over 60 are already vaccinated with the Pfizer vaccine. Therefore, in three to six weeks there should be a big drop in hospitalizations and deaths in this country (there is of course a delay between being infected and going to hospital). Other countries should follow soon after as more people become vaccinated.    Achieving herd immunity only decreases the likelihood of COVID spreading, it does not change the outcome for someone who is infected. In the US Scott Gottlieb, former FDA commissioner, estimates that around 60 million people who over 60 will take the vaccine, but after that there are many people in the US who will not. So, herd immunity may take a long time to achieve, but it does not really matter. The US manufactures both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccine locally, and in a few months more vaccine manufacturers will almost certainly come online. So, once older people are vaccinated the overloading of the health system will stop and this will happen long before the US achieves herd immunity.    Finally, the US is fortunate that the vaccine manufacturing takes place inside the country. This means that they will be able to offer vaccine to their entire population between two and four months before other developed countries like Canada, that must import all their vaccine.    To conclude, I think my chain of reasoning is both evidence based and sound. Does anyone disagree?

With 20 times more suspected than confirmed cases, this category of disease cannot be ignored simply because there was no positive PCR test result. comment_text: Re: the vaccine: I think some of the skepticism in the scientific community comes from the lack of long-term safety analysis, since these types of vaccines are so new. My parents are both physicians and while they are completely in favor of vaccination in general, they are still somewhat cautious about these new ones in particular because they just haven't been studied over years like conventional vaccines have (which we know are completely safe). This University of Cambridge page (https://www.phgfoundation.org/briefing/rna-vaccines) says: 'key consideration: Safety: better understanding of vaccine adverse effects is needed – these can include inflammation or autoimmune reactions'. I think caution is mostly warranted for people with autoimmune disorders since they may be at increased likelihood of having over-reactions. My view is, as with most things, it should be a risk-benefit analysis (how sick one would get from covid vs taking the risk of potential effects in the future), so for most people getting a vaccine is probably the safest choice. Basically to answer Grant, I think 'reasoned' skepticism comes from the fact that the effects have only been studied short-term, and that sometimes theory and practice end up not matching perfectly. (Also the huge financial race for pharmaceutical companies to get their vaccines out asap, along with everyone's impatience to see a vaccine out, isn't the most reassuring thing safety-wise) (To be clear, not arguing against getting vaccinated, just wanted to give another perspective.)

comment_text: There’s also some more things to add: here in Germany, half of received doses are currently kept aside for the second shot. In the UK and some other countries, essentially most of received vaccines are being administered more or less directly, and the second dose is expected to be administered from a timely received batch.  The second way has an obvious advantage, as more people can be vaccinated with at least a first dose, which does provide a significant level of protection after about two weeks, though not the full 95% efficacy.  However, this “just in time“ strategy is more prone to delivery or production issues.  For example, the Pfizer factory in Belgium recently started some limited reconstruction in order to ramp up their production in March, but those measures do right now slow down their production to unexpected low output. Following the “just in time“ strategy may delay administering the second dose by weeks, and those intervals haven’t been tested. Due to this, medical staff in the UK has been notified that their second dose appointments have been cancelled, but new ones will be announced to be administered within 12 weeks after the first dose. In medicine grade 3 adverse events are considered 'severe'. The fact that they are short lived is irrelevant, a car crash may last only a few seconds but it can affect the rest of your life. According to the trial result of both Pfizer and Moderna their trials did not include a.) the vaccine's ability to prevent infection, b.) to stop or slow down the spread of the virus and c.) serious mid- and long term side effects have not been studied at all. And the trials were not double blind. Both Pfizer and Moderna have indicated that their study will end around the end of 2023 at which point they will make the results public. So if you get an injection now you are taking part in a global experiment which does not mean you should not take it, just be aware of these facts and the risks that go with it.

comment_text: Thank you very much for this: it is also a delight to hear your accent for some reason! I am fond of the Indian accent. I had my vaccine yesterday and it was fine, I did have mild muscle aches today and last night, a mild headache but I understand the muscle aches are an indication that the immune response has been innitiated, so nothing to worry about. If one knows what the cause is, then I wouldn't count this as 'suffering': and it is nothing compared to the deleterious effects of the virus itself. My grandmother died of it and I think it's a real tragedy when someone reaches her age and then in the end is taken by something avoidable: I'm sure most people know someone or more then one person for whom this virus has taken there life.   Bearing this in mind I think it makes little rational sense to pass up the vaccine out of a fear of possible physical symptoms. Out of all the millions of people who have been vaccinated (about 18 million in the UK alone), there have been no documented cases of this vaccine causing death, and I don't know of any serious adverse events that have been blamed on the vaccine. It is fear caused by distrust, caused by the absence of understanding that surely leads someone to resist: so I would urge anyone to find out the facts for themselves, from sources they trust. You areprotecting not just yourself but anyone you come in to contact with. There are no known serious risks to taking it but no end of possible serious consequences for anyone who doesn't.

comment_text: For those interested, here was my experience:  I work at a nursing home in the middle of the country therefore I was able to get my first dose of the Pfizer vaccine Saturday January 2nd and the second dose on the 23rd. After the first shot my arm felt a bit sore for day and a half, but it was gone for the most part by Monday. I felt a little tired, but probably because I slept for only 4 hours the night before. After the second shot, I felt fine the day I received the shot other than a similar sore feeling where I got the shot. However I woke up on Sunday feeling like much of my energy had been sucked out of me and I kind of had the chills when first waking up, but no fever or headache, and after I got some food and some Gatorade in me I felt okay - still a bit drained but it could've been worse - the rest of the day. Monday I woke up and felt fine again and I've been good in the week-and-a-half since. Also to note I'm in my 30s, I smoke (I know, I know...), and my blood pressure could be lower. So yeah, all in all not the most fun experience of my life but I'd rather a day of feeling kind of bleh over a week or two of feeling like crap if I caught COVID.

comment_text: I got the vaccine from work, I work in a retirement and rehabilitation home so as you can guess all of our residents are at risk. The 1st shot I only had muscle aches at the injection site and in the surrounding area, the second shot I thankfully didn't get sick but the injection site was extremely swollen, hot to the touch and itchy. Within a week and with the help of some ice packs the swelling went down significantly. Its been about 2 weeks since I got the second shot and the only thing left over is a small lump at the injection site that's growing smaller every day. If you get the chance to get the vaccine I still 100% say do it, the swelling and itching was a very mild annoyance that I would gladly go through again to help control the virus. My manager got the vaccine too, he experienced flu like symptoms that were extremely bad for 1 day but he felt almost completely better the next day. Again, if you have the chance please do your part to improve our heard immunity for those who cannot get the vaccine so we can slowly get back to normal.
